name: NoLiMa benchmark (arXiv:2502.05167)
publisher: Adobe Research (Hanieh Deilamsalehy, Franck Dernoncourt, Trung Bui, Ryan A. Rossi, Seunghyun Yoon) and LMU Munich (Ali Modarressi, Hinrich Schütze)
date_published: Submitted to arXiv 2025-02-07; revised v3 2025-07-09; accepted at ICML 2025
claim_value: Across 13 state-of-the-art LLMs claiming 128K+ context support, tested from 250 to 128K tokens: most score above 90% at short context, but 11 of 13 models fall below 50% of their own short-context baseline by 32K tokens. GPT-4o, the strongest model (99.3% base score), drops to 69.7% at 32K and 56% at 128K. Models' 'effective context length' (context length at which performance stays above 85% of baseline) is far shorter than their advertised context window, in many cases 2K tokens or less.
claim_definition: A benchmark result: NoLiMa measures retrieval and reasoning over long context when the question and the 'needle' (the fact the model must find) share no literal keyword overlap and instead require inferring a latent/associative link (e.g. real-world or commonsense knowledge connecting the question's wording to the needle's wording). This is distinct from classic Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH), which allows literal/lexical matching between question and needle.
reproducibility: Public: the paper states dataset and evaluation code are released on GitHub, and the benchmark has been adopted/cited by independent follow-on work (e.g. Chroma's 'Context Rot' report, and later papers such as 'Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval'), indicating independent reuse rather than only self-reported results. Accepted at ICML 2025, i.e. peer-reviewed.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No. Adobe Research and LMU Munich are not selling a context/retrieval/vector-DB product tied to this benchmark; this is academic research, not a vendor benchmark.
conflict_notes: None found for this item specifically. One nuance worth flagging: Chroma's later 'Context Rot' report (which cites NoLiMa approvingly) also notes a limitation in NoLiMa's own design: it found 72.4% of NoLiMa's needle-question pairs require external/commonsense knowledge to bridge, meaning NoLiMa tests a blend of non-lexical matching AND general knowledge recall at once, not purely non-lexical matching in isolation. This is a critique of NoLiMa from a source that otherwise relies on it, not a contradiction of NoLiMa's headline degradation numbers.
relationship: Supports the 'context engineering matters, not just prompt engineering' framing, but from the angle of exposing a measurement gap rather than prescribing a technique. NoLiMa shows that strong NIAH scores (which can be gamed via literal keyword matching) do not mean a model can actually use long context when retrieval requires semantic/associative reasoning. This strengthens the broader context-engineering argument that just stuffing more tokens into a prompt, or trusting a vendor's advertised context window, is not sufficient; how information is presented and whether it can be found without lexical shortcuts matters a great deal.
derivative_of: Explicitly extends Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH), the earlier long-context evaluation method that tests retrieval of a fact planted in a long document. NoLiMa's stated motivation is that NIAH's literal keyword overlap between question and needle lets models rely on surface pattern matching, inflating apparent long-context competence; NoLiMa removes that lexical shortcut. NoLiMa is itself later cited and built upon by Chroma's 'Context Rot' report (2025) and by later papers probing long-context degradation (e.g. arXiv:2510.05381).
register: academic researcher, though its findings are widely cited downstream for a practitioner/engineer audience (it's one of the most-cited sources used to argue that advertised context-window sizes overstate real usable context).
notes: Verified directly against the arXiv abstract/page content (v3) and cross-checked against Chroma's Context Rot report, which both cites NoLiMa's results and offers a methodological critique of it (the 72.4% external-knowledge-dependency point). No numeric discrepancies found between the paper's own abstract/summary and how it's described in secondary sources (DigiAlps summary, Chroma report) for the core stats (99.3% to 69.7% to 56% for GPT-4o; 11/13 models below 50% of baseline at 32K).
new_angle: Adds the specific quantitative degradation curve (GPT-4o: 99.3% to 69.7% at 32K to 56% at 128K; 11/13 models below 50% of baseline at 32K) and the 'effective context length' concept (often far below advertised context window, sometimes 2K tokens or less), plus the explicit derivative relationship to NIAH and the fact that Chroma's Context Rot report both relies on and critiques NoLiMa's design (the 72.4% external-knowledge overlap point). None of this specific detail is in article_ideas.md's existing 09-27 entry.
